citation.title: credentials(7), passwd(5), group(5) — Linux man-pages 6.19; shadow(5) — shadow-utils; capabilities(7)

claims.planned: Processes carry real, effective, saved UIDs/GIDs and supplementary groups; the kernel checks numeric IDs, names are just a lookup in /etc/passwd
claims.finding: credentials(7) lists real, effective, saved set-, and (Linux-specific) filesystem user/group IDs plus supplementary group IDs, and says 'These IDs are integers'. On Linux the FILESYSTEM IDs (normally equal to the effective IDs) are what file permission checks use. The 'names are just a lookup' half is from passwd(5): utilities like ls use /etc/passwd 'to map user IDs to usernames'. Executed: a file chowned to 4242:4242 (no passwd entry) is listed by `ls -l` with the bare numbers.
claims.quote: Each process has various associated user and group IDs. These IDs are integers, respectively represented using the types uid_t and gid_t (defined in <sys/types.h>).

claims.planned: UID 0 is the superuser; privilege is tied to effective UID 0 (traditionally) and to capabilities
claims.finding: passwd(5): the root login account 'has the user ID 0'. capabilities(7): traditional UNIX distinguishes privileged processes (effective UID 0) that bypass all kernel permission checks; since Linux 2.2 that privilege is split into capabilities, a per-thread attribute. credentials(7) itself does not make the UID-0 statement — cite capabilities(7)/passwd(5).
claims.quote: privileged processes (whose effective user ID is 0, referred to as superuser or root), and unprivileged processes (whose effective UID is nonzero). Privileged processes bypass all kernel permission checks

claims.planned: /etc/passwd format: seven colon-separated fields (name:password:UID:GID:GECOS:directory:shell); world-readable; password field 'x' means hash is in /etc/shadow
claims.finding: Exactly seven fields in that order. 'should have read permission allowed for all users ... but write access only for the superuser'. Password field is the encrypted password, '*', or 'x' (hash in /etc/shadow). Empty shell field means /bin/sh. Executed: /etc/passwd is 644 root:root; first line 'root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash'.
claims.quote: Each line of the file describes a single user, and contains seven colon-separated fields: name:password:UID:GID:GECOS:directory:shell

claims.planned: /etc/shadow readable only by root (and shadow group); fields
claims.finding: shadow(5): 'must not be readable by regular users'; nine colon-separated fields: login name, encrypted password, date of last change (days since 1970-01-01), minimum age, maximum age, warning period, inactivity period, account expiration date, reserved. A password field starting with '!' is locked; '!' or '*' alone means no password login is possible. The 'shadow group' detail is distro practice, not in the man page — verified by running: Ubuntu 24.04 has /etc/shadow 640 root:shadow (same on alpine:3.20).
claims.quote: This file must not be readable by regular users if password security is to be maintained. Each line of this file contains 9 fields, separated by colons

claims.planned: A child process inherits its parent's credentials
claims.finding: fork(2) child inherits copies of the parent's user and group IDs; across execve(2) the real IDs and supplementary groups are preserved while effective and saved IDs may change (set-user-ID programs). Executed: as uid 1001, bash -> bash -> sh all report 1001.
claims.quote: A child process created by fork(2) inherits copies of its parent's user and groups IDs. During an execve(2), a process's real user and group ID and supplementary group IDs are preserved; the effective and saved set IDs may be changed, as described in execve(2).

extra_findings.fact: What each ID is for: real = who owns the process; effective = permission checks for IPC (and files on most UNIXes); saved set-ID = lets a set-user-ID program drop and regain privilege.
extra_findings.quote: Real user ID and real group ID. These IDs determine who owns the process.

extra_findings.fact: Linux filesystem UID/GID: what file permission checks actually use; tracks the effective ID automatically.
extra_findings.quote: These IDs, in conjunction with the supplementary group IDs described below, are used to determine permissions for accessing files; see path_resolution(7) for details. Whenever a process's effective user (group) ID is changed, the kernel also automatically changes the filesystem user (group) ID to the same value.

extra_findings.fact: Supplementary groups limit: 65536 since Linux 2.6.4 (32 before).
extra_findings.quote: since Linux 2.6.4, a process can be a member of up to 65536 supplementary groups.

extra_findings.fact: User IDs also govern who may send signals (kill(2)), set scheduling parameters, and how resource limits are counted.
extra_findings.quote: when determining the permissions for sending signals (see kill(2));

extra_findings.fact: Capabilities are per-thread and date from Linux 2.2.
extra_findings.quote: Starting with Linux 2.2, Linux divides the privileges traditionally associated with superuser into distinct units, known as capabilities, which can be independently enabled and disabled. Capabilities are a per-thread attribute.
It should have read permission allowed for all users (many utilities, like ls(1) use it to map user IDs to usernames), but write access only for the superuser.

These days many people run some version of the shadow password suite, where /etc/passwd has an 'x' character in the password field, and the encrypted passwords are in /etc/shadow, which is readable by the superuser only.

extra_findings.fact: Field details: GID is the PRIMARY group (others come from /etc/group); directory sets HOME; shell sets SHELL and defaults to /bin/sh when empty; an empty password field means no password is asked.
extra_findings.quote: This is the numeric primary group ID for this user. (Additional groups for the user are defined in the system group file; see group(5)).
group_name:password:GID:user_list ... user_list a list of the usernames that are members of this group, separated by commas.
If the password field begins with an exclamation mark !, the password is locked.

extra_findings.fact: '*' / '!' in the shadow password field: no password login, but other login methods still work.
extra_findings.quote: If the password field contains a string that is not a valid result of crypt(3), for instance ! or *, the user cannot use a UNIX password to log in. However, the user may log in the system by other means.

extra_findings.fact: Observed account files on the reference image.
extra_findings.quote:
$ stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /etc/group /etc/gshadow -> 644 root:root /etc/passwd ; 640 root:shadow /etc/shadow ; 644 root:root /etc/group ; 640 root:shadow /etc/gshadow
$ grep '^root' /etc/shadow -> root:*:20707:0:99999:7:::
(new useradd account) alice:!:20717:0:99999:7:::
(as alice) cat /etc/shadow -> cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied

extra_findings.fact: ubuntu:24.04 ships a non-root account 'ubuntu' with UID/GID 1000, so the first `useradd` user gets 1001; debian:bookworm-slim has no UID-1000 user. Matters for bind-mount ownership and for 'run as uid 1000' harness configs.
extra_findings.quote: $ grep -E ':(1000|0):' /etc/passwd -> root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash / ubuntu:x:1000:1000:Ubuntu:/home/ubuntu:/bin/bash ; id alice -> uid=1001(alice) gid=1001(alice) groups=1001(alice)

extra_findings.fact: Numeric IDs are what is stored: a file owned by a UID with no passwd entry is shown numerically.
Credentials are inherited down the process tree.

teaching_notes: credentials(7) is about process IDs, not about root: the 'UID 0 is superuser' sentence lives in capabilities(7) and passwd(5), so cite those. Linux nuance worth one sentence: file checks use the filesystem UID, which shadows the effective UID. The 'root and shadow group' readability of /etc/shadow is Debian/Ubuntu/Alpine packaging (640 root:shadow, observed), while the man pages say only 'superuser only' / 'must not be readable by regular users'. Surprise for container work: ubuntu:24.04 already contains user ubuntu at UID 1000.
